title: Exercise in Alzheimer's Disease: Functional Biomarkers
official: Physical Exercise in Alzheimer's Disease: Impact on Functional Biomarkers and the Muscle-Gut-Brain Axis
summary: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the leading cause of dementia worldwide and involves systemic alterations beyond the brain, such as loss of muscle strength, chronic low-grade inflammation, and gut microbiome dysbiosis. Physical exercise is a promising non-pharmacological therapy, and velocity-based resistance training has proven safe and effective in older adults. However, the effects of performing resistance exercises at high versus moderate velocity in people with AD remain unknown, and human evidence on how exercise modulates the gut microbiome in AD is very limited. This study aims to assess and compare the effects of two velocity-based resistance training modalities (high load at moderate velocity and moderate load at high velocity) versus usual care on the gut microbiome, systemic inflammation, plasma biomarkers, biological age, and intrinsic capacity in older adults with mild-to-moderate AD, using cognitively healthy older adults as a reference group.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria - participants with Alzheimer's Disease

* Age ≥ 60 years
* Medical diagnosis of mild or moderate Alzheimer's disease based on clinical criteria and plasma biomarkers.
* Able to perform physical activity according to medical assessment
* Written informed consent from the participant or, when capacity is insufficient, from the legal representative

Inclusion Criteria - cognitively healthy reference group

* Age ≥ 60 years
* No medical diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or cognitive impairment according to clinical criteria
* Preserved functional autonomy
* Able to perform physical activity according to medical assessment
* Written informed consent

Exclusion Criteria:

* Major surgery in the previous 3 months
* Total functional dependence
* Uncontrolled neuromuscular disease or severe heart disease
* Antibiotic, probiotic or corticosteroid treatment in the 4 weeks before biological sample collection
